content: Alternative periodic tables are unique representations of chemical elements that differ from the traditional Mendeleev periodic table. These alternative designs are often created for educational purposes, as the standard periodic table does not fully capture all the relationships and correlations between chemical elements. One notable example is Theodor Benfey's periodic table from 1960, where the elements are arranged in a two-dimensional spiral starting from hydrogen. This spiral folds around two distinct islands representing the transition metals and the lanthanides and actinides. Additionally, a superactinide island is preemptively included in this design. Similarly, in the Chemical Galaxy (2004), the elements are also arranged in a spiral pattern. The Extended Periodic Table, proposed by Glenn T. Seaborg in 1969, includes hypothetical elements with atomic numbers up to 218. In this table, helium is placed among the group 2 elements. Timothy Stowe's Physicist's Periodic Table is a three-dimensional representation where the axes correspond to the principal quantum number, orbital quantum number, and orbital magnetic quantum number. In this model, helium is again classified as a group 2 element. Paul Giguère's three-dimensional periodic table consists of four interconnected billboards. The first billboard displays group 1 elements on the front and group 2 elements on the back, excluding hydrogen and helium. At a 90° angle, the second billboard contains groups 13 to 18 on its front and back. Two additional billboards, also positioned at 90° angles, include the remaining elements. In the field of superatoms, clusters of atoms exhibit properties similar to those of single atoms from other elements. It has been suggested that the periodic table could be extended with a second layer to accommodate these cluster compounds. L. Rich proposed a periodic table where certain elements appear in multiple locations when appropriate. For instance, hydrogen is shown to share properties with group 1 elements due to its valency, with group 17 elements because it is a non-metal, and with the carbon group due to similarities in chemical bonding and electronegativity. In this version of the periodic table, carbon and silicon are also grouped with titanium and zirconium. The primary aim of alternative periodic tables is to emphasize specific chemical or physical properties of elements that may not be immediately apparent in traditional periodic tables. Some designs focus on highlighting the nucleon and electronic structures of atoms by altering the spatial relationships or representations of elements. Other tables aim to showcase the historical timeline of chemical element isolation by humans.
